newsitem.title: USA: U.S Treasury expected to announce CMB sale Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: U.S Treasury expected to announce CMB sale Tuesday.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury on Tuesday is expected to announce an offering of cash management bills (CMBs) for sale later this week, analysts said.
But unlike past years, when the Treasury sold CMBs in early March and again in April, one CMB might be enough to get the government thorugh its usual seasonal cash shortfall, they added.
The CMB announcement is seen coming at 1430 EST/1930 GMT, the same time the Treasury is slated to detail Monday's three- and six-month bill auctions.

The Treasury likely will sell the CMBs on Thursday for settlement on March 3, and maturing shortly after the April 15 personal tax filing deadline -- probably April 17 or April 21. Analysts said the 45- or 49-day CMB should be in the $25.0 billion range.

In the past, the Treasury has needed at least two CMBs to get through this season when it sends out billions of dollars in tax refunds. But, said UBS Securities LLC money market analyst Kathy Bostjancic, the Treasury might not need another one in April like it usually does.

The government has had "strong tax receipts due to an increase in employment and income," she said. "They still run into kind of a lull in cash balances. So, until (the April 15) tax date, they'll need some extra cash."
Bostjancic said it is pretty normal to do a CMB in early March, but since it could be the only one of the season, it will be larger than usual.

In 1996, the Treasury offered four CMBs, noted Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc: $6.0 billion on March 1, $9.0 billion on March 14, $30.0 billion on April 1, and $25.0 billion on April 3.
A year earlier, the Treasury offered two CMBs worth $33.0 billion -- one in early March and the other in early April.
Flanagan said the Treasury will probably come back with another CMB in late March or early April to cover Social Security payments. "But I don't think they need something that dramatic," he said.
Flanagan said the Treasury's inflation-indexed bond sale earlier this year, as well as a return to a quarterly 30-year bond auction, takes care of the need for a string of CMB auctions.
In addition, analysts expect the Treasury to increase the size of its weekly bill sales to $27.0 to $28.0 billion from Monday's $26.0 billion.
